context_before.text: A simplified screening test, therefore appears to be available in which, at a fixed potential in the intermediate range, the temperature of the solution is increased until pitting is observed. This technique would appear to take advantage of the fact that an intermediate potential, such as +500 mV (SCE), is common to all of the alloys regardless of their relative resistances with respect to temperature and the steep slope of the temperature-potential curves would suggest a well defined transition.

In this series of experiments, the experimental apparatus was the same as that used in the previous investigation.1 In this case, freshly abraded samples of the experimental alloys listed in Table 1 were exposed in nitrogenated 3.5% (0.6M) NaCl pH3 solution and were allowed to corrode freely forfive minutes,usually assuming a potential of -365 to -370 mV (SCE). The potential was then rapidly increased to a value of +500 mV (SCE) and held potentiostatically. After a five minutes waiting period, during which the current density decreased to the range 1 to $3 \ \mu \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$, the temperature of the solution was increased at the rate of 0.6 C per minute. The temperature at which the current density increased sharply to a value of $1 0 \mu \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ (the criterion for pit initiation in Figure 1) was considered to be the temperature at which pitting began and was designated $\Upsilon _ { 5 0 0 }.$ For each alloy, multiple runs were carried out.

context_after.text: The results are summarized in Table 2 in terms of minimum, maximum, and average $\mathtt { T } _ { 5 0 0 }$ values and are graphically displayed in Figure 2 with the curves from Figure 1. Figure 2 clearly demonstrates the power of this technique in quickly and easily screening a series of alloys for relative resistance to pitting. The excellent correlation confirms the earlier data and takes advantage of the steep slope of the potential-temperature curves in describing relative pitting resistance in terms of a temperature, a parameter with possible design significance if the effects of testing rate can be taken into account.

section_title.text: $\mathbf { F e C l } _ { 3 }$ Exposure Tests at Various Temperatures

context_before.text: Shape changes in Figure 1 of the type proposed above would indicate that long term pitting tests should be insensitive to potential over the whole intermediate potential range, but very dependent upon test temperature. Data produced at +500 mV (SCE) is apparently near the postulated point of rotation of the transition section of the curves and should therefore be applicable in predicting long term pitting behavior. To some extent this hypothesis is substantiated by the data of Figure 2 which correlate as well for the less resistant alloys (short exposure times) as for the more resistant alloys (exposure times approaching one hour). Further corroboration was obtained by means of a series of longer exposures carried out as a function of temperature in a solution with oxidizing power in the intermediate potential range.

Coupons of the experimental alloys were exposed in 10% (0.6M) FeCl3 solution for 24 hours at a temperature of 27.5 C. The potential of this solution, measured on bright platinum, was +695 mV (SCE) and the pH was approximately 1. As pointed out by Bond and $\mathbb { L i z l o v s }, { \mathbf 3 }$ polarization effects result in a somewhat lower potential being measured on the corroding sample, but still within the intermediate potential range defined by Figure 1. After this 24 hour exposure, coupons were examined visually to see whether pitting had occurred. Edge, end grain or crevice attack, which occurred in some cases, was not considered. The bath temperature was then increased by 2.5 C and the coupon reimmersed for another 24 hours. This process was continued until pitting was observed.

context_before.text: Experimental confirmation of the proposed vertical temperature-potential curves in the intermediate potential region to describe infinitely slow scan rates was obtained by a series of 66 hour exposure experiments. Samples of 317L stainless steel were exposed to the following solutions of similar chloride activities but very different oxidizing power: 16% sodium hypochlorite (domestic bleach) containing 3.5% NaCl, 10% FeCl3, and 5% potassium ferricyanide containing 3.5% NaCl. In all cases, pitting was observed at a temperature of 30 C or higher, but not at à temperature of 27.5 C or lower. The strong dependence on temperature and not on potential suggests that there exists for each wholly austenitic steel a critical pitting temperature below which the steel will not pit regardless of potential and exposure time. The data presented here are considered to approximate such a parameter.

In Figure 3, this critical pitting temperature, within the limits of accuracy of the techniques described here, is plotted as a function of the Mo content of the various steels, both experimental and commercial. In the case of FeCl3 exposure tests, the low temperature end of the error bars plotted in Figure 3 represents the temperature at and below which pitting was not observed, while the high temperature end indicates the temperature at and above which pitting was observed after a 24 hour exposure. The minimum and maximum Tsoo values are also plotted in Figure 3 as error bars. In each case, these bars represent the degree of uncertainty in determining the critical pitting temperature by these techniques. context_after.text: Although the critical pitting temperature of a steel has been obtained in three different but apparently equivalent ways, the preferred method appears to be by the use of FeCl3 exposures. This technique minimizes testing rate effects, differentiates between pitting and crevice and end grain attack, uses samples of any geometry, and requires a minimum of electronic gadgetry. Regardless of the technique used, however, the correlation shown in Figure 3 appears to be a valid and workable way of describing the pitting susceptibility of wholly austenitic alloys in terms of a parameter with design significance.
